{#vixl} # Discussion

{#y8gj} The etiology of strabismus following the implantation of glaucoma drainage devices is multifactorial and may result from various factors including the mass effect of the implant, implant-induced restriction, adherence of retro-orbital fat, intraoperative trauma to extraocular muscles, muscle scarring, or displacement of the muscle pathway. Extensive encapsulation around the implant can limit ocular movement in the direction of the implant, while scarring and contractures may pull the eye towards it [@w:w9].

{#zagc} The most common form of postoperative strabismus observed is restrictive strabismus . The preferred implant position is typically in the superotemporal quadrant of the orbit, as this area offers more available space and reduces the likelihood of interference with the oblique muscles. Consequently, exotropia and/or hypertropia of the ipsilateral eye have the highest incidence. Additionally, inferior placement of drainage implants appears to be more likely to cause diplopia, particularly in reading positions, due to the altered visual alignment [@w:w10].

Added an explicit comparison with previous studies at the end of this paragraph, keeping the original sentence and its existing citation (14–16) unchanged.

Newly added: "Comparable mechanisms have been described in previous studies: Muñoz and Parrish attributed the restrictive strabismus after Baerveldt implantation to a bleb-induced increase in the muscle length–tension curve together with a posterior fixation effect from scarring behind the implant, whereas Dobler-Dixon et al. reported generalized restrictions, acquired Brown syndrome and extraocular muscle palsies in similar proportions after double-plate Molteno implantation, indicating that both mechanical and muscle-related mechanisms contribute."

Rationale: the two cited series support the multifactorial claim made here — Muñoz and Parrish (Arch Ophthalmol 1993) documented a restrictive pattern after Baerveldt implantation and proposed bleb-related length–tension change plus posterior fixation from scarring, and Dobler-Dixon et al. (Arch Ophthalmol 1999) found generalized restrictions, acquired Brown syndrome and muscle palsies in similar proportions after double-plate Molteno implantation, i.e. both mechanical and muscle-related mechanisms. Two references were added for these (neither was in the reference list).
